name: The Candle Waste

detectability.signature: Broad-spectrum thermal bloom with characteristic coronal flicker; long-range sensors read it as a second, angry sun that isn't there.

proximity: Hull surfaces ionize and glow faintly amber
Communications degrade into a wash of static and ghost voices
contact: Ablative shielding boils away within minutes
External sensor arrays fuse or blind permanently
prolonged_exposure: Structural members anneal and sag in the heat gradient
Crew radiation exposure exceeds survivable limits without heavy shielding

behavior.cycle: 19-day storm cycle: six days building, nine days raging, four days of treacherous calm

phenomena: Arcs of plasma leap between magnetic filaments like slow lightning
The whole volume glows deep orange, bright enough to read by at its edge
Ships report their shadows cast onto nothing by the storm's inner light
Metallic dust drawn into the storm burns in brief green flares
hazards: Thermal loading exceeding hull tolerances during the rage phase
Radiation dose rates dangerous even behind standard shielding
Magnetic turbulence capable of flipping small craft end over end
opportunities: The calm phase offers a rare window to harvest ionized heavy elements from the storm's fringe
Storm-warmed volatiles condense into harvestable frost on the outer boundary markers
known_incidents: The ore hauler Bright Answer misjudged the calm phase by two hours; her crew was recovered from the boundary markers, her hull was not.
Racing pilots hold an unsanctioned tradition of touching the storm's edge during first light of the build phase; one dies roughly every decade.
description: From a distance the Candle Waste looks like a sun caught mid-detonation and frozen there: a roiling sphere of orange plasma half an astronomical unit across, wrapped in slow coils of magnetized fire. Its light is steady enough to navigate by and warm enough to feel through a hull, which has fooled exactly enough ships to have a name for the phenomenon. Sensors paint it as a thermal wall with no source behind it.

The storm breathes on a nineteen-day cycle. Six days of gathering brightness, nine days of open fury when arcs leap between filaments and anything inside the boundary begins to cook, then four days of calm so still and clear that veterans distrust it more than the rage. The pattern holds well enough to schedule around, poorly enough to kill anyone who schedules carelessly.

Charted sixty million years into its tantrum by a survey crew that lost a probe and nearly a ship, the Waste has been a fixed hazard on every regional map since. The Bright Answer disaster gave it its safety protocols, and the racers who graze its edge give it its legends. Harvest crews time the calm phases like farmers timing a river, and the storm takes its customary tithe regardless.

These days the boundary is strung with warning buoys and the calm phases are logged publicly, which has made the Waste profitable rather than merely famous. Research platforms study why the storm renews itself at all, since nothing visible feeds it. And the old question remains open, asked anew whenever the cycle runs long: what happens the day it doesn't stop building?
